en: The Discourse to Sigālaka (Siṅgālasutta), Dīgha Nikāya 31.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.
Now at that time Siṅgālaka, the householder’s son, having risen early and departed from Rājagaha, with wet clothes and wet hair, joined his palms and paid homage to the various directions:
the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the nadir, and the zenith.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
The Blessed One saw the householder’s son Siṅgālaka, who had risen early and departed from Rājagaha, with wet clothes and wet hair, with palms joined together,
worshipping the various directions— the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the downward direction, and the upward direction.
Having seen him, he said this to Siṅgālaka the householder’s son:
“Why is it, householder’s son, that having risen early and departed from Rājagaha, you are now—with wet clothes and wet hair—worshipping the various directions with palms joined:
the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the downward direction, and the upward direction?”
“Venerable sir, when my father was dying, he said to me:
‘My dear son, you should pay homage to the directions.

Venerable sir, out of respect for, reverence for, honor toward, and veneration of my father’s words, I rise early, depart from Rājagaha, and with wet clothes and wet hair, with palms joined together, I pay homage to the various directions.”
“The eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the downward direction,
and the upward direction. “Householder’s son, in the discipline of the Noble One, the six directions are not to be venerated in this way.”
“But how, venerable sir, are the six directions to be revered in the discipline of the Noble One?
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma as to how the six directions are to be revered in the discipline of the Noble One.
“In that case, householder’s son, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” Siṅgālaka the householder’s son replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“When, householder’s son, a noble disciple has abandoned four defilements of action, by means of four [things]...”
He does not commit evil deeds through these six bases, nor does he pursue the six doors to the loss of wealth.
Thus, having abandoned fourteen evils and covering the six directions, he practices for victory in both worlds.
For him, this world is mastered, and the world beyond is mastered as well.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
2. Four Corruptions of Action:
For whom are the four corruptions of action abandoned?

“Householder’s son, the destruction of life is a defilement of action; taking what is not given is a defilement of action; sexual misconduct is a defilement of action; false speech is a defilement of action.
These four defilements of action have been abandoned by him.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“The taking of life, the taking of what is not given,
and false speech are so called.”
“Going to another’s wife, the wise do not praise.
3. The Four Points.
“In what four ways does one not commit an evil deed?

One commits an evil deed when acting out of favoritism, one commits an evil deed when acting out of ill will, one commits an evil deed when acting out of delusion, and one commits an evil deed when acting out of fear.
But when, householder’s son, a noble disciple acts neither out of favoritism, nor out of ill will, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear;”
“By these four grounds, one does not perform evil karma.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“He who transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame diminishes.”
Like the moon in the dark fortnight,
he who does not transgress the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
“His fame increases, like the moon during the waxing fortnight. 4.
Six Gateways to Decline.
“What are the six doors to the loss of wealth that one does not frequent?

Devotion to the use of fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence, O householder’s son, is a door to the loss of wealth; devotion to wandering through the streets at improper times is a door to the loss of wealth;
attending fairs is a door to the loss of wealth; devotion to the practice of gambling, which is the basis for negligence...”
Devotion to evil friends is a gateway to the ruin of wealth; devotion to laziness is a gateway to the ruin of wealth.
5. Six dangers of liquor and spirits:
Householder’s son, there are these six dangers in devotion to the basis of negligence through liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.

The loss of wealth visible in this very life, the increase of quarrels, the breeding ground for diseases, the cause of ill-repute, the exposure of one’s private parts—this is the sixth point: the weakening of wisdom.
These, householder’s son, are the six dangers in the pursuit of the occasion for negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants. 6. Six Dangers in Roaming at Unfit Times:
Householder’s son, there are these six dangers in the practice of wandering for alms at improper times:
one’s own person is unprotected and unguarded; one’s wife and children are unprotected and unguarded;
one’s property is unprotected and unguarded; one is suspected of evil deeds; and false accusations are leveled against one.
It grows, and one stands at the forefront of many states of suffering.
These, householder’s son, are the six dangers in the practice of wandering for alms at improper times.
7. The six dangers in wandering among assemblies.
Householder’s son, there are these six dangers in attending festivals:
where is the dancing? Where is the singing? Where is the instrumental music? Where is the recitation? Where is the hand-clapping? Where is the drumming?
These, householder’s son, are the six dangers in attending festivals.
8. Six Disadvantages of Heedlessness in Gambling "There are, householder’s son, these six disadvantages in the practice of indulgence in gambling.

One who wins engenders enmity; one who loses grieves over his wealth; there is an immediate loss of property; one's word does not carry weight in the assembly; one is despised by friends and colleagues; and one is shunned by those with whom one has marriage alliances."
‘This person is a gambler; he is not capable of supporting a wife.
These, householder’s son, are the six dangers in the practice of gambling and heedlessness. 9.
The six dangers in associating with evil friends:
Householder’s son, there are these six dangers in following evil friends:
those who are debauchees, those who are drunkards, those who are gluttonous, those who are double-dealers, those who are deceivers, and those who are violent—they become one's friends and companions.
These, householder’s son, are the six dangers in following evil friends.
10. Six Disadvantages of Laziness:
“Householder’s son, there are these six disadvantages in the pursuit of laziness.

Thinking ‘it is too cold,’ one does not work; thinking ‘it is too hot,’ one does not work; thinking ‘it is too late,’ one does not work; thinking ‘it is too early,’ one does not work; thinking ‘I am too hungry,’ one does not work; thinking ‘I am too full,’ one does not work.”
As he dwells thus, making excuses for his duties, wealth that has not yet arisen does not arise, and wealth that has already arisen goes to ruin.
These, householder’s son, are the six dangers in the pursuit of laziness.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke further:
“There is one called a drinking companion,
and there is one who is a close friend.”
He who is a companion when misfortunes have arisen is a true friend.
Sleeping late and consorting with another's wife—
The procreation of offspring, harmfulness,
evil friends, and extreme stinginess—
these six conditions cause a person to decline.
Having evil friends, evil companions,
and evil conduct and associations,
one falls away from this world and the next.
Both of these destroy men:
women, dice, liquor, dancing and singing,
sleeping by day, and attending to oneself at the wrong time.
Evil friends and extreme stinginess—
these six conditions cause a person to perish.
They play with dice and drink liquor.
Women are as dear to others as their own lives;
one who serves the base and does not serve the noble wanes like the moon in the dark fortnight.
But he who is destitute, homeless, and possesses nothing,
yet drinks when thirsty after coming to a tavern—
he plunges into debt like one plunging into water.
He will quickly bring confusion upon himself by being one whose habit is to sleep during the day and who regards the night as the time for waking.
It is possible for one who is constantly intoxicated and addicted to drink to live at home; [but not so] for one who thinks,
"it is too cold" or "it is too hot."
"This is too late," they say;
thus, while their work is neglected,
the opportunities pass by for those young men.
The one who does not regard cold and heat as anything more than blades of grass,
while performing his human duties—

“Thus, one does not dwell in happiness. “Householder’s son, these four are to be known as enemies in the guise of friends. What four? (1) One who speaks pleasant words but does not act accordingly; (2) one who praises you to your face but disparages you behind your back; (3) one who shares your wealth when it is present but does not share it when it is absent; and (4) one who associates with you for their own gain but not for yours. These four, householder’s son, are to be known as enemies in the guise of friends.”
One who takes what is not given should be understood as a friend in the guise of a friend; one who is a master of words should be understood as a friend in the guise of a friend;
one who speaks only pleasant words should be understood as a friend in the guise of a friend; and one who is a companion in misfortune should be understood as a friend in the guise of a friend.
Householder’s son, one who takes what is not given should be understood as a friend in the guise of a friend for four reasons.
He takes what belongs to others;
he desires much for the sake of little;
he performs his duty out of fear.
He serves for the sake of his own interest.
Householder’s son, by these four grounds one should recognize a false friend who takes only for himself.
Furthermore, householder’s son, by four grounds one should recognize a false friend who is merely a friend in words.
He greets one with reference to the past; he greets one with reference to the future; he treats one with affection for no purpose; and he points out misfortune regarding present duties.
Householder’s son, it is by these four grounds that a friend in appearance who is actually a foe, being a mere lip-friend, is to be recognized.
Furthermore, householder’s son, it is by four grounds that a friend in appearance who is actually a foe, being a flatterer, is to be recognized.
He approves of his evil deeds, he approves of his good deeds, he speaks in praise of him to his face, and he speaks in dispraise of him behind his back.
Householder’s son, by these four grounds one should recognize a pleasant-speaker who is a non-friend appearing in the guise of a friend.
Furthermore, householder’s son, by four grounds one should recognize a companion in misfortune who is a non-friend appearing in the guise of a friend.

“He is a companion in the pursuit of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence; he is a companion in the pursuit of wandering about at improper times and through the streets; he is a companion in attending fairs;

he is a companion in the pursuit of gambling, which is a basis for negligence. Householder’s son, by these four grounds one should recognize a companion in the lower realms as a non-friend who merely has the appearance of a friend.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“A friend who takes only for himself,
and a friend who is merely a talker;”
He who speaks what is pleasing,
and he who is a friend in times of misfortune—
these four are enemies.
Having understood this, the wise person should avoid it from afar,
just as one would a dangerous path.
12. Friends Who Are Kind “Householder’s son, four kinds of friends who are kind should be recognized.

A helpful friend should be recognized as a kind friend; a friend who shares in both pleasure and pain should be recognized as a kind friend; a friend who speaks what is beneficial should be recognized as a kind friend; and a compassionate friend should be recognized as a kind friend.”
Householder’s son, a helpful friend who is well-disposed is to be recognized by four grounds.

He protects one when one is negligent; he protects the property of one who is negligent; he becomes a refuge for one who is afraid; and when there are duties or tasks to be performed, he provides twice as much wealth.
Householder’s son, it is by these four grounds that a helpful friend who is well-disposed is to be recognized.
Householder’s son, a friend who is easy to please and shares in one's joys and sorrows is to be recognized by four grounds:
he reveals his secrets to you, he guards your secrets, he does not abandon you in times of misfortune, and he would even sacrifice his own life for your sake.
Householder’s son, it is by these four grounds that a friend who is easy to please and shares in one's joys and sorrows is to be recognized.
Householder’s son, a friend who speaks for one’s welfare and is well-disposed should be recognized by four grounds:
he restrains one from evil, establishes one in what is wholesome, makes known what has not been heard, and points out the path to heaven.
Householder’s son, it is by these four grounds that a friend who speaks for one’s welfare and is well-disposed should be recognized.
“Householder’s son, a compassionate friend who is easy to please should be recognized by four grounds.
He does not rejoice in one’s misfortune, he rejoices in one’s prosperity, he restrains one when speaking dispraise, and he commends one when speaking praise.
By these four grounds, householder’s son, a compassionate friend who is easy to please should be recognized.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“The friend who is helpful, and...”
He who is a friend in both happiness and suffering,
he who is a friend who speaks of what is beneficial,
and he who is compassionate toward friends.
Having understood that there are these four kinds of friends,
the wise person should attend upon them with proper care.
Like a mother her own biological son,
the wise one endowed with virtue shines like a fire in the water.
As he gathers wealth,
moving like a bee,
his riches go toward accumulation.
Just as an anthill is built up,
so too a householder, having accumulated wealth,
becomes self-sufficient within his family.
One should divide one's wealth into four parts;
thus indeed does one bind friends.
With one part, one should enjoy one's wealth.
One should employ two types of kamma;
one should cause a fourth to be stored away for times of misfortune.”
13. The Chapter on Covering the Six Directions “And how, householder’s son, is a noble disciple one who covers the six directions?
These six directions, householder’s son, should be understood.
The eastern direction should be understood as one’s parents; the southern direction should be understood as one’s teachers;

the western direction should be understood as one’s children and spouse; the northern direction should be understood as one’s friends and companions; the downward direction should be understood as one’s slaves and laborers;
and the upward direction should be understood as ascetics and brahmins.
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a son attend upon his mother and father, the eastern direction:

‘I will support those who supported me; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will take charge of the inheritance; or else, when they have passed away, I will offer gifts for the sake of the deceased.
Householder’s son, when a son attends upon his mother and father, the eastern direction, in these five ways, they show compassion toward him in five ways."
They restrain him from evil; they establish him in what is wholesome; they train him in a craft; they unite him with a suitable wife; and at the proper time, they hand over the inheritance.
In these five ways, householder’s son, are parents served by their son as the eastern quarter; and in these five ways do they show compassion for their son.
Thus this eastern quarter is covered for him, secure and free from fear.
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a pupil serve his teacher as the southern direction:
by rising [to greet him], by attending upon him, by being willing to listen, by rendering service, and by receiving the craft with diligence.
Householder’s son, when a pupil serves his teacher as the southern direction in these five ways, the teacher shows compassion toward that pupil in five ways:"

They discipline those who are well-disciplined; they cause them to grasp what is well-grasped; they provide thorough instruction in all crafts; they provide for their friends and kinsmen; and they provide protection for them in all directions.
Householder’s son, when preceptors are attended to by a pupil from these five standpoints, they show compassion toward that pupil through these same five standpoints.
In this way, that southern direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a husband attend to his wife as the western quarter:
by honoring her, not disparaging her, by not being unfaithful, by entrusting her with authority, and by providing her with ornaments.
Householder’s son, when a wife is attended to by her husband in these five ways as the western quarter, she in turn shows compassion toward her husband in five ways:"
She is well-organized in her duties, she has won over her attendants, she is not unfaithful, she protects what has been gathered, and she is skillful and untiring in all tasks.
Householder’s son, when a wife is established as the western direction by her husband through these five ways, she shows compassion toward her husband through these same five ways.
In this way, her western direction is protected, secure, and free from fear.
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a clansman attend to his friends and companions as the northern direction:
by giving, by kindly speech, by acting for their welfare, by impartiality, and by not being deceitful.
Householder’s son, when friends and companions are attended to by a clansman in these five ways, they in turn show compassion toward that clansman in five ways:"

They protect one who is negligent; they guard the property of one who is negligent; they become a refuge for one who is afraid; they do not abandon one in times of misfortune; and they honor his offspring.
It is by these five grounds, householder’s son, that friends and companions established as the northern direction show compassion toward a clansman.
In this way, this northern direction is covered for him, secure, and free from fear.
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a master attend to his slaves and laborers as the lower direction:

by arranging their work according to their strength, by providing food and wages, by nursing them when they are sick, by sharing extraordinary delicacies with them, and by granting them leave at the proper time.
Householder’s son, when slaves and laborers are attended to by a master in these five ways, they show compassion toward that master in five ways:"
They rise before him, retire after him, take only what is given, perform their work well, and bring fame and reputation.
In these five ways, householder’s son, are slaves and laborers served by their master as the lower direction; and in these five ways do they show compassion for their master.
In this way, his lower direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a clansman attend upon ascetics and brahmins as the zenith:

with bodily action imbued with loving-kindness, with verbal action imbued with loving-kindness, with mental action imbued with loving-kindness, by opening his doors to them, and by providing material gifts.
When ascetics and brahmins are attended upon in these five ways, householder’s son, they show compassion for that clansman in six ways:"

“They restrain one from evil, establish one in what is wholesome, show compassion with a wholesome mind, cause one to hear what has not been heard, clarify what has been heard, and point out the path to heaven.
Householder’s son, in these five ways do recluses and brahmins stand as the zenith toward a clansman; and in these six ways they show compassion for that clansman.
Thus is that zenith covered over for him—secure and free from fear.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“Mother and father are the eastern direction;”
Teachers are the southern direction;
wife and children are the western direction;
friends and colleagues are the northern direction.
Servants and laborers below,
and ascetics and brahmins above—
one should pay homage to these directions.
A householder who is content with his own family,
wise, endowed with virtue,
gentle, and eloquent;
Humble in conduct and free from arrogance,
such a person gains renown;
being industrious and untiring, he attains his goal.
He does not tremble in times of misfortune;
the wise man of unbroken conduct gains such fame.
One who is inclusive, a maker of friends,
generous, free from stinginess;
a leader, a guide, and one who persuades others.
Such a person obtains glory:
generosity, pleasant speech,
and purposeful conduct in this world.
And equanimity toward all things,
as is appropriate in each case—
these indeed are the means of integration in the world.
Like the linchpin of a moving chariot,
were these means of integration not present,
even a mother would not, for the sake of her son, restrain him from evil.
One might receive honor or worship because of one's father,
or as a result of one's children;
yet these are merely forms of attachment.
The wise perceive correctly;
therefore they attain greatness and become worthy of praise.
When this was said, Siṅgālaka the householder’s son said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or one might show the way to one who is lost, or one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The Siṅgāla Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
